meta.title: EU AI Act Basics
meta.thesis: EU AI Act Basics is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A product team must classify an AI feature before launch and understand which obligations apply. By the end, they should be able to build or review EU AI Act risk classification worksheet for a customer-facing assistant, measure risk category and obligations documented before release, and catch the failure where the team treats all AI systems as equal and misses high-risk obligations.

objectives: Explain the risk-based structure in practical terms.

Build a dated classification memo for one education tool.

blocks.title: The law classifies systems by use

spans.text: Problem anchor: Agentic Learning Studio wants to offer an AI lesson coach to EU schools. The same model can be low-risk in a private drafting demo, transparency-relevant in a public chatbot, or potentially high-risk if used to evaluate students or influence educational access. The intended purpose matters.

As of June 23, 2026, the EU AI Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. It uses a risk-based structure that includes prohibited practices, high-risk systems, transparency obligations, and general-purpose AI model provisions. This lesson teaches product literacy, not legal advice; a real launch needs qualified counsel.
Date-sensitive note: obligations phase in over time. Prohibited-practice rules and GPAI-related rules have different dates than many high-risk obligations.

items.text: Product framing: ask what the system is intended to do to people or decisions.
Engineering framing: classification turns into evidence work: logs, docs, data governance, human oversight, monitoring.
Governance framing: record assumptions, role, reviewer, and date because facts and guidance can change.

spans.text: System: AI lesson coach for secondary-school learners in the EU. Intended purpose: explain concepts, give practice feedback, and recommend next lessons. Not intended purpose: grade students, decide admission, allocate scholarships, or discipline learners. Users: students, teachers, school administrators. Actor role: likely deployer for a school using a third-party model, but provider duties may arise if packaging and marketing a system under the Studio brand.

Initial risk note: tutoring and feedback require transparency, data governance, and human override. If the system is used to evaluate learning outcomes or influence access to education, counsel must review high-risk classification and obligations before launch.

blocks.title: Classification first step
blocks.prompt: What should an AI Act worksheet start with?

options.text: The system intended purpose, users, geography, actor role, and possible risk category.
A promise that all AI use is low risk.

blocks.explanation: Risk analysis starts with use context and role, not the model name alone.

modules.title: Know the risk buckets and actor roles
modules.sub: Separate prohibited, high-risk, transparency, GPAI, provider, and deployer questions.
modules.summary: The AI Act creates different duties depending on risk category and the actor placing or using the system.
objectives: Describe the main risk buckets without overclaiming.
Connect risk class to evidence requirements.

spans.text: A practical worksheet separates questions. Is any prohibited practice implicated? Is the intended purpose in a high-risk area? Does the user need to know they are interacting with AI or seeing generated content? Does the product rely on a general-purpose AI model with its own documentation chain? Which party is provider, deployer, importer, distributor, or product manufacturer?

Actor role matters because the same company may have different duties when building a system, customizing it, deploying it internally, or reselling it. Product teams should not guess role from vibes; they should document facts and route the memo to counsel.

cells.text: Practices the regulation bans or restricts severely
Could the system manipulate, exploit vulnerability, or enable banned scoring or biometric use?
Block by design and document why feature is out of scope
Does intended purpose affect education, employment, credit, law enforcement, migration, or similar listed domains?
Risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, human oversight, monitoring

options.name: Transparency or GPAI

cells.text: Must users know AI is involved, or do upstream model obligations matter?
Notices, model cards, summaries, provider documentation, content labeling where relevant

options.whenToUse: Use before launch copy and vendor review.

spans.text: If the lesson coach only suggests practice resources and clearly lets teachers override it, the worksheet may focus on transparency, privacy, safety, and vendor governance. If the same system scores learners and those scores influence placement, access, or certification, the risk analysis changes materially and high-risk obligations may be in scope.
This reinforces module 1: intended purpose is not decorative metadata. It decides which evidence, controls, and legal questions matter.

modules.title: Turn classification into controls and evidence
modules.sub: Map the likely obligations to documentation, logging, oversight, and monitoring artifacts.
modules.summary: A readiness memo becomes useful when it names the controls and evidence a team must maintain.
objectives: Connect risk class to implementation artifacts.
Avoid treating compliance as a one-time checkbox.

spans.text: For a serious AI system, evidence lives in ordinary engineering artifacts: requirements, data governance records, evaluation results, incident reports, logs, human-oversight flows, monitoring dashboards, vendor documentation, and change-management notes. The goal is to prove the system was designed, tested, launched, and updated responsibly.

Even when a system is not high-risk, the same artifacts help. Transparency notices, data minimization, user feedback, and model-version logs make it easier to explain behavior and respond to incidents.

blocks.title: Worked evidence plan for the lesson coach

spans.text: Controls: clear AI-use notice in the product; teacher-visible settings for feedback mode; no automated grading without explicit separate review; source citations for factual claims; learner-data retention rules; prompt and retrieval version logs; human escalation for contested feedback; monitoring for unsafe content, hallucinations, and fairness slices.

Evidence: classification memo, vendor/model documentation, data inventory, eval report, safety release checklist, incident playbook, and dated legal-review note. The memo says which controls are product commitments and which are legal assumptions awaiting counsel.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Build the evidence you would want during an incident or regulator question.
blocks.useWhen: Use formal evidence management when the system faces EU users, educational institutions, sensitive data, or user-impacting recommendations.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid launching on an informal promise that the model provider alone handles compliance.

blocks.title: AI Act worksheet sanity check
blocks.code:
worksheet = {
    "system": "EU lesson coach",
    "intended_purpose": "practice feedback and lesson recommendations",
    "not_intended": ["grading", "admissions", "discipline"],
    "eu_users": True,
    "actor_role_guess": "deployer/provider facts need counsel",
    "uses_student_data": True,
    "human_oversight": "teacher can review and override",
    "legal_review_required": True,
}

required = ["intended_purpose", "eu_users", "actor_role_guess", "human_oversight"]
missing = [k for k in required if not worksheet.get(k)]
assert not missing, f"missing AI Act classification facts: {missing}"
if worksheet["eu_users"] and worksheet["uses_student_data"]:
    print("route to privacy and legal review before launch")

spans.text: This is a product-readiness check, not legal classification software. Its job is to make missing facts visible and route the decision to qualified review.

predictThenReveal.prompt: What changes if the same system starts assigning official course-placement scores?
predictThenReveal.answer: The intended purpose changes, so the risk analysis and likely evidence obligations must be reopened before launch.

blocks.title: Verify an AI-generated EU AI Act summary

spans.text: Check that any AI-generated summary cites Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 or official EU guidance, states the date of the claim, distinguishes risk categories, avoids legal advice certainty, and tells the team when counsel must review actor role and intended purpose.

items.text: Does it distinguish provider and deployer questions?
Does it date phase-in assumptions as of June 23, 2026?
Does it connect classification to concrete evidence artifacts?
Does it avoid saying an education product is automatically low-risk or high-risk without facts?

blocks.title: Legal certainty trap
blocks.prompt: What is unsafe about an AI-generated claim that "this EU education AI is definitely compliant"?

options.text: Compliance depends on facts, role, intended purpose, dates, implementation evidence, and legal review.
It includes too many source links.

blocks.explanation: Regulatory readiness needs dated assumptions and qualified review, not blanket confidence.

blocks.title: Retrieval prompt for the whole lesson

spans.text: Answer this from memory: "How do I start an EU AI Act readiness review for an AI product?" Include intended purpose, users, EU exposure, actor role, risk bucket, transparency, GPAI dependency, data governance, human oversight, logging, monitoring, dated assumptions, and legal review.

Spaced recall: module 1 classified the lesson coach by intended purpose. The final memo must reopen if the product becomes a grader, admissions aid, employment screener, or other user-impacting system.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Treat AI Act readiness as a living memo with counsel-owned conclusions.
blocks.useWhen: Use the worksheet for EU-facing, school-facing, workplace, customer, or high-impact deployments.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid relying on a one-time classification after adding new uses, new markets, new vendors, or automated decisions.

blocks.title: Capstone: write a one-page classification memo

spans.text: Pick one AI feature. Fill in system name, intended purpose, excluded uses, user groups, geography, actor role facts, risk category questions, transparency needs, data-governance controls, human oversight, logs, monitoring, vendor dependencies, legal-review owner, and date. Add a red box for facts that would change the classification.
Next rung: connect this to the safety release checklist so regulatory questions become launch gates rather than afterthoughts.

hallucination.label: Hallucination
hallucination.laymanDefinition: A generated claim that lacks support or is false.
hallucination.technicalNote: For education or customer-facing tools, hallucination risk affects transparency, accuracy controls, and human review expectations.

prompt_injection.label: Prompt injection
prompt_injection.laymanDefinition: A way untrusted text can manipulate an AI system.
prompt_injection.technicalNote: Prompt injection matters to AI Act readiness when it affects robustness, logging, cybersecurity, or harmful outputs.

guardrail.label: Guardrail
guardrail.laymanDefinition: A control used to meet a risk or transparency obligation.
guardrail.technicalNote: In an AI Act readiness worksheet, guardrails include human oversight, logging, data governance, technical documentation, transparency notices, and post-market monitoring.

privacy.label: Privacy
privacy.laymanDefinition: Personal-data protection and data minimization duties around AI systems.
privacy.technicalNote: AI Act work does not replace GDPR or local privacy review; data governance and lawful basis still need counsel.

owasp.label: OWASP
owasp.laymanDefinition: A security reference for LLM application threats.
owasp.technicalNote: OWASP is not the AI Act, but its LLM risks can supply concrete controls for cybersecurity and misuse portions of a readiness plan.

risk_register.label: Risk register
risk_register.laymanDefinition: A table of use-case risks, classification assumptions, controls, evidence, and owners.
risk_register.technicalNote: The AI Act worksheet should feed the risk register with dated assumptions and legal-review notes.
